A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TaTS framework, CTR phenomenon and TT-Wasserstein metric. Their text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v2 reports original forecasting and imputation experiments on Time-MMD, including Tables 2–3 and detailed results and ablations in Appendix E.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and reports additional FNSPID/FNF forecasting results, fusion and text-corruption studies, and TT-Wasserstein stability analyses.

M1.justification: The default text encoding, MLP projection, concatenation, objectives and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. Section 5.2 adds optional gated-residual and cross-attention fusion variants, plus a mitigation procedure that drops noisy texts and substitutes placeholders.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from nine Time-MMD datasets to eighteen datasets by adding six FNSPID company-stock series and FNF Bitcoin-price, web-traffic and electricity-demand forecasting (Tables 4, 15–16 and 28). v3 also introduces evaluation with missing textual inputs. Forecasting and imputation remain the principal tasks.

E2.justification: v3 adds GPT4MTS to the N-BEATS, N-HiTS, TCN and ChatTime comparison, and introduces TFHTS, MCD-TSF and TeR-TSF comparisons using those works' reported scores (Table 12). The standalone numerical-only iTransformer entry in v2 Table 5 is omitted from the expanded comparison, although unimodal comparisons remain elsewhere.

E3.justification: Appendix B.1 introduces a separate comparison with 36/96/192-step history windows, three horizons per sampling frequency, dataset exclusions and average-rank aggregation. New ablations vary fusion, embeddings, text-drop rates and spectral processing. Original default hyperparameters remain unchanged. FNSPID settings are inconsistent: Table 15 lists horizons 6/8/10/12, while Table 28 reports only 6/12.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's existing sensitivity and shuffling studies, v3 tests whether alternative fusion helps, how missing text affects forecasts, and whether dropping corrupted text mitigates noise (Tables 6–9). Appendix A.1 tests TT-Wasserstein configuration sensitivity, Appendix E.7 compares sentence embeddings with average pooling, and Appendix D.4.3 reports leakage audits.

E5.justification: v3 first reports block-bootstrap uncertainty for TT-Wasserstein, with a stated bootstrap sample size of 10 and ± values in Table 11. The prose calls these confidence intervals, but the caption identifies standard deviations; confidence level and block length are unspecified. Forecasting seed and repeated-run reporting remains unchanged.

E6.justification: v3 adds benchmark scores, concurrent-method rankings, robustness results and text-encoding costs, while retaining the original main and detailed Time-MMD results. Shuffling summaries change alongside control aggregation, preventing a same-setting performance interpretation. New Table 28 also introduces a conflicting Traffic/PatchTST/12-step MSE of 0.361; 0.204 remains in Table 21, matching v2 Table 12.

T1.justification: New Appendix C.2 derives text-encoding cost O(t_token × l × T) under an assumed per-token processing cost and average text length. The TT-Wasserstein definition, frequency-analysis mathematics and periodicity propositions and proofs remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: identifying CTR through the PRH perspective, quantifying alignment with TT-Wasserstein, and improving forecasting and imputation through plug-in TaTS without modifying backbone architectures. Broader experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations for similar performance across fusion architectures and possible downweighting of noisy text. Appendix B.2 adds guidance for missing and misaligned texts, including an argument that small temporal shifts preserve frequency structure. The original CTR explanations and limitations remain; the shift-tolerance argument is not accompanied by a new lead–lag experiment.

D1.justification: Appendix D.4.3 newly documents chronological 80/10/10 splits, causal input masking, publication-time alignment and manual leakage audits. Other additions disclose spectral defaults, one-time text-embedding computation and costs, and new dataset statistics. Code access, hardware and default hyperparameters remain unchanged; these disclosures do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

R1.justification: v3 expands positioning against contemporary multimodal forecasters in Appendix B.1 and adds temporal-reasoning and agentic-system discussion, including MTBench, TSAIA and TimeXL, in Section 6. It also adds FNSPID, FNF and GPT4MTS references while removing broader graph and multiview citation material. This substantially refocuses the research context.

P1.justification: v3 condenses portions of the introduction and method explanation, folds Sections 4.1–4.2 into Section 4, revises experiment headings and adds appendix subsections. The overall narrative and section order remain stable. Affiliation/header wording and citation style also change.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redrawn to distinguish frozen text encoding from temporal modeling. The compact baseline comparison becomes expanded Tables 4 and 28, accompanied by new displays for robustness, metric stability, concurrent methods, dataset statistics and encoding analyses. The ICLR template and display placement change broadly; all other plotted images are retained.

improvement.justification: Broader benchmark sources, controlled fusion and missing-text tests, and leakage-prevention disclosures strengthen v2's limited cross-source validation and practical robustness evidence. The benefit is constrained by new reporting problems: inconsistent FNSPID horizons, conflicting entries in Table 28, and bootstrap standard deviations described as confidence intervals. Excluding datasets because of performance gaps also limits the strength of the concurrent-method comparison.
